'''Manuel Polo y Peyrolón''' (1846–1918) was a Spanish writer, theorist, academic, and politician. He is best known as the author of five novels falling in between [[romanticism]] and [[Realism (arts)|realism]]; classified as part of [[costumbrismo]], they are currently considered second-rate literature. As a philosopher he stuck to neo-[[Thomism]] and focused mostly on confronting [[Krausism]]. In education he represented Catholic [[regenerationism]], fiercely pitted against the [[Francisco Giner de los Ríos|Liberal]] current. In politics he was active within [[Carlism]]; his career reached its peak during his 1896–1898 term in the [[Congress of Deputies]] and his 1907-1915 terms in the [[Senate (Spain)|Senate]].

==Family and youth==
[[File:Vega del Tajo.JPG|thumbnail|left|Alto [[Maestrazgo]]]]
There is little known about Polo's ancestors. His paternal forefathers were related to [[Aras de los Olmos|Aras de Alpuente]], a town in the [[Valencia province]]; in the 17th century some Polos served there as local notaries.<ref>''Aras de Alpuente. Guia del Archivo Municipal'', Valencia 2000, p. 9</ref> His father,  Domingo Polo y Polo (died 1859),<ref>Javier Esteve Martí, ''La política antiliberal en España bajo el signo del nacionalismo: el padre Corbato y Polo y Peyrolón'' [PhD thesis Universitat de València], Valencia 2017, p. 17; see also Roberto Sanz Ponce, ''La Sierra de Albarracín y Polo y Peyroloñ: historia de una relación ascética'', [in:] ''Rehalda'' 13 (2010), p. 25</ref> also originated from [[Aras de los Olmos|Aras]].<ref>''Apuntes biográficos'', [in:] Manuel Polo y Peyrolon, ''Quien mal anda, ¿cómo acaba?'', Valencia 1890, p. 7</ref> He worked as property registrar in [[Belchite]] and according to his son he was among the founders of the Carlist daily ''[[:es:La Esperanza (periódico)|La Esperanza]]''.<ref>Esteve Martí 2017, p. 17</ref> During the [[First Carlist War]] he sided with the [[Legitimists#Spanish Bourbons|legitimists]] and served as secretary to general [[:es:José María de Arévalo|José María Arévalo y Reguero]].<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 25</ref> Following the Carlist defeat he had to abandon his job and settled in Cañete, a village on the western slopes of [[Montes Universales]], a southern ridge of [[Sistema Ibérico]]. Located in the Castillan [[Province of Cuenca]], the area bordered the region of [[Aragón]] and formed part of what was once known as Alto [[Maestrazgo]]. Polo y Polo  practiced as a local lawyer.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 19</ref>  Manuel's mother, María Peyrolón Lapuerta, was born in Aragon, on the other sides of the sierra slopes; she originated either from [[Calomarde, Aragon|Calomarde]]<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 19</ref> or from [[Gea de Albarracin]].<ref>Polo y Peyrolón 1890, p. 7</ref> The couple had at least two sons, Manuel and Florentino; María died during childbirth in 1853.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 19</ref> Some time in the mid-1850s Domingo Polo developed very serious health problems and pledged that in case of recovery he would dedicate his life to God; indeed he later entered an unspecified religious order and became a friar.<ref>B. de Artagan [Reynaldo Brea], ''Políticos del carlismo'', Barcelona 1912, p. 112</ref> 
[[File:Gea de Albarracín antiguo cuartel.jpg|thumb|[[Gea de Albarracín]], current view]]
Since the mid-1850s Manuel and his younger brother were looked after by their maternal aunt Concepción.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 19, the aunt became his second mother, Javier Urcelay Alonso, ''Introducción'', [in:] ''Memorias políticas de M. Polo y Peyrolón (1870-1913)'', Madrid 2013, {{ISBN|9788499405872}}, p. 17</ref> Spending most of his childhood and youth with relatives in [[Gea de Albarracín]],<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 11</ref> he considered himself a [[Teruel|turolense]]<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 19</ref> and viewed Sierra de Albarracín as his "{{Lang|es|patria chica}}" (little homeland).<ref>Esteve Martí 2017, p. 18</ref> He was brought up in a fervently Catholic environment<ref>''Polo y Peyrolón, Manuel (1846 -1918)'' entry at mcnbiografias.com</ref> and inherited a [[Traditionalism (Spain)|Traditionalist]] political outlook from his father; his first childhood lectures were Carlist booklets and periodicals.<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12</ref> Following his early education in Albarracin, he frequented the institute in Valencia;<ref>Esteve Martí 2017, p. 18</ref> exact dates are unclear, though most likely his college days were in the early 1860s. According to one source he majored in philosophy and literature at [[:es:Universidad de Madrid|Universidad Central]] in [[Madrid]] and in civil and canon law at [[University of Valencia|Universidad de Valencia]].<ref>mcnbiografias.com, see also cover of his works, available [https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Polo_y_Peyrolon,_Elementos_de_etica,.jpg here]</ref> Guided by [[Miguel Vicente Almazán]],<ref>Carles Sirera Mirrales, ''Neocatolicismo y darwinismo en las aulas: el caso del instituto provincial de Valencia'', [in:]  ''Ayer'' 81 (2011), p. 251</ref> Manuel would later gain PhD laurels in philosophy.<ref>Manuel Polo y Peyrolon, ''Elementos etica o filosofia moral'', Valencia 1882</ref> According to another author, he studied both law and literature in Valencia;<ref>Esteve Martí 2017, p. 18</ref> none of the sources consulted provides the date of his graduation. Following a brief and temporary stint as assistant professor of metaphysics in Valencia in 1868–69,<ref>Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 251</ref> he returned to Aragón and successfully applied to Instituto de Segunda Enseñanza de [[Teruel]], where he began teaching psychology, logic, and ethics in 1870.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 20, Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 11</ref> Manuel Polo y Peyrolón never married and had no children.<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12</ref>

==Novelist==
[[File:Los mayos, Polo y Peyrolon.jpg|thumbnail|180px|left|Los Mayos, 1885]]
Polo's first literary work, {{Lang|es|Realidad poética de mis montañas}}, appeared in 1873.<ref>full title ''Realidad poética de mis montañas. Costumbres de la Sierra de Albarracín''</ref> Except that it was a collection of short stories<ref>''Los Mellizos'', ''El sí de una serrana'', ''La tío Levítico'', ''Lo que puede una mujer'', Jose Manuel Vilar Pacheco, ''Breve noticia de obras literarias y escritores de la Sierra de Albarracín'' available [http://cecalbarracin.files.wordpress.com/2009/01/obras_literar_y_-escritores_sa_jm_villar.pdf here]</ref> instead of a [[novel]], it revealed characteristics marking his later works: traditional themes, a simple plot and clear educational purpose, with narration set in the provincial milieu of [[Sierra de Albarracín]], painted with attention to detail and with a focus on local customs typical rather of an ethnographical study.<ref>actually, the volume contained also ''Vocabulario para la inteligencia de los provincialismos, palabras anticuadas, familiares ó poco conocidas y frases oscuras contenidas en estos Cuadros''</ref> All these features were developed in Polo's first novel, ''Los Mayos'' (1878),<ref>full title ''Los Mayos. Costumbres populares de la Sierra de Albarracín''</ref> a rural love story intended as a praise of loyalty and fidelity<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 23</ref> and considered his best work,<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12</ref> translated into Italian and German.<ref>see ''Libros recibidos'' section of ''Revista de Aragon'', 20 (1879), available [http://ifc.dpz.es/recursos/publicaciones/31/08/RevistaDeAragon1879-20.pdf here]</ref> The consecutive ones, {{Lang|es|Sacramento y concubinato}} (1884)<ref>full title ''Sacramento y concubinato. Novela original de costumbres aragonesas''</ref> and {{Lang|es|Quién mal anda, ¿cómo acaba?}} (1890) assumed a more militant tone, aimed against liberal and secular lifestyles.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 23</ref> {{Lang|es|Pacorro}} (1905)<ref>full title ''Pacorro. Novela de costumbres serranas''</ref> confronted the deeds of a young liberal with the virtues of a young Carlist, cast against the background of a small town undergoing the turbulent period of 1868–1876.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 24</ref> The last of Polo's major literary works, {{Lang|es|El guerrillero}} (1906),<ref>full title ''El guerrillero. Novela tejida con retazos de la historia militar carlista''</ref> revealed more threads of an adventure story; set during [[Third Carlist War]], it was heavily based on wartime recollections of his brother Florentino.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 24</ref> Polo's shorter stories remain scaled-down versions of his novels.<ref>like ''Seis novelas cortas'' (1891) or ''Alma y vida serrana, costumbres populares de la Sierra de Albarracín (serie de cuentos)'' (1910)</ref>

Among his contemporaries Polo was appreciated usually by those sharing a similar traditional outlook, such as [[Emilia Pardo Bazán]]<ref>Jesus Bregante, ''Diccionario espasa. Literatura española'', Madrid 2003, {{ISBN|8467012722}} p. 753; relations between Polo and Baztan soured as she later accused him of plagiarism, see mcnbiografias.com</ref> and his friends [[Marcelino Menéndez y Pelayo|Marcelinó Menéndez y Pelayo]]<ref>Paula Lázaro Izquirerda, ''Lengua patria y dialectos regionales: una convivencia necesaria en el pensamiento de Manuel Polo y Peyrolon'', [in:] ''Rehalda'' 5 (2007), p. 28</ref> and [[José María de Pereda]].<ref>see Jose Maria de Pereda, ''Cuarenta cartas ineditas a Manuel Polo y Peyrolon'', Santander 1990, {{ISBN|9788485429875}}</ref> A conservative literary review, ''[[:es:La Ilustración Católica|Ilustración Católica]]'',<ref>he started to co-operate with the periodical in 1880, María del Carmen Servén Díez, ''La ilustración católica frente a la novela: 1877-1894'', [in:] ''Revista de literatura'' 127 (2002), p. 231;</ref> identified him as a brilliant follower of [[Fernán Caballero]],<ref>Ulpiano Lada Ferreras ''La narrativa oral literaria: estudio pragmático'', Oviedo 2003, {{ISBN|3935004362}}, 9783935004367, p. 96</ref> classified his writings as a "{{Lang|es|novela de familia}}" (family novel) and hailed his prose as "{{Lang|es|restauradora de la novela castellana en los tiempos modernos}}" (the restorer of the Castilian novel in modern times).<ref>Servén Díez 2002, p. 229</ref> Noted for authenticity "which does not disfigure reality", his [[Realism (arts)|realism]] was appreciated as an antidote to [[Naturalism (literature)|naturalism]] – the trend he consciously opposed<ref>compare his theoretical study ''El naturalismo ¿ es un signo de progreso ó de decadencia en la literatura?'', published in 1885</ref> - and "the venom of [[Émile Zola|Zola]]".<ref>Servén Díez 2002, p. 231</ref> By favourably disposed contemporaries he was put next to Fernán Caballero, de Pereda, [[:es:Francisco Navarro Villoslada|Francisco Navarro Villoslada]], [[Julio Alarcón y Meléndez]], [[Juan Valera y Alcalá-Galiano|Juan Valera]] and [[Luis Coloma|padre Coloma]];<ref>Servén Díez 2002, p. 234</ref> critics dubbed him a "{{Lang|es|mamarracho literario}}" (literary monstrosity.)<ref>loosely translatable as "literary clown", an insult cointed by [[Azorín|José Martinez Ruiz]] in the 1890s, quoted after Felipe Pedraza Jimenez, Milagros Rodriguez Caceres, ''Manual de literatura española'', vol. IX, Tafalla 1987, {{ISBN|8485511182}}, p. 537</ref> 
[[File:Cabecera de la revista La Ilustración Católica.jpg|thumbnail|280px|[[:es:La Ilustración Católica|''La Ilustración Católica'']]]]
The limited popularity of Polo's works hardly outlived their author. Even in the early 20th century he was only marginally mentioned by historians of [[Spanish literature]];<ref>in his massive work ''Historia de la lengua y literatura castellana'', Julio Cejador y Frauca marginally mentions Polo y Peyrolón in volume IX (''Segundo periodo de la epoca realista''), Madrid 1918, but ignores him in volumes X/XI (''Epoca regional y modernista''), Madrid 1919</ref> later on he went into oblivion,<ref>he is straightforwardly mentioned as a second-rate novelist by Santiago Sebastian, ''Aportación de Polo y Peyrolón a la Etnologia turolense'', [in:] ''Aragon'' 1958, p. 6</ref> though was occasionally acknowledged in anthologies.<ref>excerpts from his ''Historia de un ochavo moruno'' (1884) were placed in Jose Bergua (ed.), ''Las mil mejores paginas de la lengua castellana. Antologia de prosistas'', Madrid 1969, pp. 301-303</ref> Today he is missing even in fairly detailed studies written either by Spanish<ref>Iris M. Zavala, ''Historia y critica de la literatura espanola'', vol. 5 (''Romanticismo y realismo''), Barcelona 1982, {{ISBN|847423185X}}, Juan Luis Alborg, ''Historia de la literatura española'', vol. 6 (''Realismo y naturalismo. La novela''), Madrid 1996, {{ISBN|8424917936}}</ref> of foreign scholars,<ref>D. L. Shaw, ''Historia de la literatura española'', vol. 5 (''El siglo XIX''), Barcelona 1972, {{ISBN|8434483564}}</ref> though he is noted by some dictionaries.<ref>compare Ricardo Gullon (ed.), ''Diccionario de Literatura Española y Hispanoamericana'', vol. 2, Madrid 1993, {{ISBN|8420652482}}, p. 1312, or Bregante 2003, p. 753</ref> He is usually situated in between [[romanticism]] and [[Literary realism|realism]],<ref>Mariano Baquero Goyanes, ''El cuento español: del romanticismo al realismo'', Madrid 2012, {{ISBN|9788400072131}}, p. 78</ref> falling into the [[costumbrismo]] (or {{Lang|es|realismo costumbrista}}) trend,<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12</ref> also a good representative of {{Lang|es|novelas de tesis}}.<ref>Bregante 2003, p. 753</ref> It is noted that his conventional, meager plots can hardly support the weight of nagging moralising objectives, especially given the repetitive nature of his works.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 22, [[Magdalena Aguinaga Alfonso]], ''El costumbrismo de Pereda: innovaciones y técnicas narrativas'', Oviedo 1996, {{ISBN|3930700816}}, 9783930700813, p. 154</ref> On the other hand, his novels are appreciated as inexhaustible sources of perfectly captured anecdotes and customs, few readers admitting even some charm.<ref>''Polo y Perolón, Manuel'' entry on ''Gran Enciclopedia Aragonesa'' online,  available [http://www.enciclopedia-aragonesa.com/voz.asp?voz_id=10315 here] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205020659/http://www.enciclopedia-aragonesa.com/voz.asp?voz_id=10315 |date=2014-12-05 }}</ref> Apart from realism,<ref>occasionally Polo's realism also slipped into somewhat cruel naturalism, see Baquero 2012, p. 78</ref> he is credited for introducing new narrative techniques.<ref>Baquero 2012, p. 77</ref> He is also among the best-known authors contributing to [[Carlism in literature]] from the legitimist perspective.

==Scholar and philosopher==
[[File:Polo y Peyrolon, Elementos de etica,.jpg|thumbnail|160px|left|Polo's textbook, 1882]]
Polo taught psychology, logic, and ethics in the Teruel college for 9 years. Harassed for his pro-Carlist sympathies,<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, pp. 21-22</ref> he decided to leave Aragon. Following a successful application and selection process,<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 22</ref> he assumed the same chair at [[Instituto de Segunda Enseñanza]] in Valencia in 1879,<ref>most sources claim he moved in 1879; Sanz, however, notes (p. 14) that "Polo saca la cátedra del Instituto de Valencia [sic!] y traslada su residencia a la capital del Turia" in 1880</ref> where he kept teaching until the early 20th century. Member of [[Asociación de Catedráticos Numerarios]],<ref>Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 257</ref> he was active in a number of Spanish and foreign scholarly institutions.<ref>like [[Sociedad Económica de Amigos del País]], Comision de monumentos historicos y artisticos de la provincia de Valencia, Academia Filosofico-Medica de Santo Tomas de Aquino de Roma, Academia Cientifica de Bruselas, M. Polo y Peyrolon, Elementos de etica o filosofia moral, Valencia 1882</ref> His career was crowned in 1908, when he joined [[Real Academia de la Historia]].<ref>mcnbiografias.com, see also Agustín Fernández Escudero, ''El marqués de Cerralbo (1845-1922): biografía politica'' [PhD thesis], Madrid 2012, p. 420</ref>

During his Valencia tenure Polo wrote textbooks for students of philosophy: ''Elementos de psicología'' (1879), ''Elementos de lógica'' (1880), ''Elementos de Ética'' (1880); ''Elementos de Ética o Filosofía Moral'' (1882), ''Elementos de Filosofía Moral'' (1889), ''Lógica elemental'' ( 1902) and ''Ética elemental'' (1902),<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 11</ref> in use also in other scholarly centres across the country.<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 11, mcnbiografias.com</ref> He did not develop any original philosophical contribution himself; apart from works on history and general overviews, Polo is known for confronting some trends forming the liberal educational mindset, especially [[Krausism]] and [[Darwinism]]. His stance is classified as [[neo-Thomist]] or ''[[Neocatólicos|neocatolicismo]]'' in philosophy<ref>Sirera Mirrales 2011, pp. 251-2; some name him the follower of [[Jaime Balmes]], see Federico Martínez Roda, ''Valencia y las Valencias: su historia contemporánea (1800-1975)'', Valencia 1998, {{ISBN|8486792894}}, 9788486792893, p. 190</ref> and as regeneracionismo político-educativo in pedagogy.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2011</ref>

Polo's repudiation of Krausism developed in the course of his teaching career and stemmed from his growing interest in pedagogy and education in general.<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 11</ref> During the last decades of the 19th century, Krausism became a philosophical powerhouse of liberal Spanish politics, represented mostly by [[Francisco Giner de los Ríos|Francisco Giner del Rios]] and [[Instituto Libre de Enseñanza]].<ref>also by [[Francisco Pi y Margall]], [[Emilio Castelar]], [[:es:Manuel Pedregal y Canedo|Manuel Pedregal y Canedo]], [[Rafael Altamira y Crevea|Rafael Altamira]], Paweł Skibiński, ''Historia a siwadomosc nardowa. Próba analizy historiografii hiszpanskiej drugiej połowy XIX stulecia'', [in:] ''Przegląd Historyczny'' 91 (2000), pp. 225-230</ref> Its principal intellectual antagonist was Menendez y Pelayo.<ref>Skibiński 2000, pp. 227-228</ref> His friend Polo remained rather a proponent and did not construct his own anti-Krausian theory, though his vehemence gained him the description of "{{Lang|es|grande enemigo de la barbarie krausista}}" (great enemy of Krausist barbarism),<ref>Enrique Sanchez Reyes, ''Estudios y discursos de crítica histórica y literaria. Siglo XIX. Críticos y novelistas. Estudios regionales. hispanistas y literaturas extranjeras'', Madrid 1942, quoted after ''Biblioteca Virtual Menénded Pelayo'', available [http://www.larramendi.es/menendezpelayo/i18n/corpus/unidad.cmd?idUnidad=100174&idCorpus=1000&posicion=1 here]</ref> especially as Spanish Krausism, initially avoiding direct confrontation with the Church, later assumed a decisively challenging tone.<ref>Skibinski 2000, pp. 228-229</ref> Fiercely advocating Catholic integrity as a basis of public education,<ref>see for instance his 1913 defence of teaching [[Catechism]] in public schools, see Roberto Sanz Ponce, ''La enseñanza del Catecismo ayer y hoy: las reflexiones del senador Polo y Peyrolón'' at formacioncontinua.com (2013), available [http://formacioncontinua.ucv.es/congreso/wp-content/uploads/2013/i/La_ense%C3%B1anza_del_Catecismo-Roberto_sanz.pdf here] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141204180340/http://formacioncontinua.ucv.es/congreso/wp-content/uploads/2013/i/La_ense%C3%B1anza_del_Catecismo-Roberto_sanz.pdf |date=2014-12-04 }}</ref> he nevertheless recognized the necessity of incorporating elements from the liberal mainstream; some scholars even maintain that Polo was completely integrated in the liberal system of education.<ref>Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 241</ref>
[[File:La serpiente y la lima, en La Ilustración Católica.jpg|thumbnail|180px|Anti-krausist cartoon, 1881]]
Another characteristic feature of Polo's outlook was his position towards [[evolutionism]],<ref>embodied in ''Contra Darwin: supuesto parentesco entre el hombre y el mono'', published in 1881; Emilia Pardo Bazán accused this work of plagiarism, see mcnbiografias.com</ref> though opinions on his stance differ. Some view it as an exemplary obscurantist Catholic reaction to scientific progress,<ref>mcnbiografias.com</ref> dismissed as "{{Lang|es|involucionismo, integrismo, tradicionalismo e ideario reaccionario}}" (involutionism, fundamentalism, traditionalism and [[reactionary]] ideology.)<ref>a contemporary student notes that "Polo's demons"  - liberals, krausists, darwinists and freemasons – were the same demons that haunted [[francisco Franco|Franco]], Lázaro Izquirerda 2007, p. 29</ref> Some suggest that his neo-Thomism was not an abrupt rejection of advances produced by science,<ref>Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 251-2</ref> as Polo tried to work out a conciliatory approach.<ref>"Como muchos pensadores católicos, Peyrolón confiaba supeditar el empirismo científico a la fe católica de una forma conciliadora. Pero la dificultad de esta tarea se acrecentó con la difusión del darwinismo en el último tercio del siglo XIX por la intensa polémica intelectual que suscitó al tratarse de la primera controversia científica de alcance mundial que transcurrió, al mismo tiempo, ante los académicos versados en la materia y el público general", Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 253</ref> Though his stance on Darwinism is portrayed as "aggressive and intolerant attack",<ref>see the opinion of José María López Piñero, quoted after Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 256</ref> others consider it in line with scientific standards of the era, systematic and posing questions  - like those related to hereditary transmission or variability patterns  –  which remained unanswered until the 1920s.<ref>Thomas F. Glick, ''Darwin en España'', Valencia 2010, {{ISBN|9788437078182}}, p. 53</ref> A detailed study suggests that Polo engaged in the discourse not so much to challenge evolutionary theory,<ref>in Valencia Polo had to share the scholarly ambience with Emilio Ribera, one of the top naturalists, Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 254</ref> but to confront secularism which used it as a ram against the Spanish Catholic outlook.<ref>Sirera Mirrales 2011, p. 260</ref>

==Politician==
[[File:Flag of Cross of Burgundy.svg|thumbnail|left|Carlist standard]]
Polo commenced his political career in 1870, speaking at local meetings in Sierra de Albarracín.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 20</ref> During the Third Carlist War he supported the insurgents as an [[:es:ojalatero|ojalatero]],<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 22; Polo's younger brother Florentino served in Carlist troops as adjutant and secretary to general [[Manuel Marco y Rodrigo]]</ref> placed under police surveillance with most of his property embargoed.<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 21</ref> Facing restrictions and fearing for his life, he temporarily went into hiding;<ref>Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 21</ref> even following the Carlist defeat in 1876 he was harassed at his workplace in Teruel for a long time.<ref>he had to enter repetitive oposiciones a cátedra to get his contract prolonged, Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 22</ref>

In the 1880s he contributed to the legitimist cause mostly as a novelist, propagating Carlist virtues of his protagonists, and as a professor, lambasting liberal ideas<ref>his public activities were guided by 4 principles: fighting liberalism, especially its Catholic version embodied in the "unionistas", defending the Church against liberal secularisation attempts, fighting socialism and republicanism among the urban proletariat and the Carlist legitimism, Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 18-19</ref> disseminated by [[Jews]]<ref>Solange Hibbs-Lissorgues, ''Imágenes del judío y antisemitismo en la literatura y la prensa católicas del siglo XIX'', [in:] Lucienne Domergeu (ed.), ''Pueblo, nación y elites. España contemporánea'', Paris 1996,  pp. 167-188</ref> and [[freemasonry]].<ref>see Polo's ''La masonería española'' lecture, delivered at 5t Congreso Católico Español in Burgos in 1899, Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 25-26</ref> In 1891<ref>''Archivo diplomático y consular de España'', Madrid, 24.08.92, n. 418, p. 1661, quoted after ''Manuel Polo y Peyrolón 1846-1918'' entry at filosofia.org, available [http://www.filosofia.org/ave/001/a005.htm here]. However, he is not listed as an official Carlist candidate by Fernández Escudero 2012, pp. 237-238</ref> and 1893<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 249</ref> he lost campaigns to [[Cortes Generales|Cortes]] and was finally victorious in 1896.<ref>see official Cortes service available [http://www.congreso.es/portal/page/portal/Congreso/Congreso/SDocum/ArchCon/SDHistoDipu/SDIndHistDip?_piref73_1340024_73_1340023_1340023.next_page=/wc/servidorCGI&CMD=VERLST&BASE=DIPH&FMT=DIPHXLDA.fmt&DOCS=1-25&DOCORDER=FIFO&OPDEF=Y&QUERY=%2890450%29.NDIP. here]</ref> In parliament he focused on education, opposing Liberal secularisation plans<ref>according to Polo, Canalejas did more for Carlism than dozens of meetings and leaflets, Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 15</ref> and promoting local languages in schools.<ref>with the purpose to teach castellano, Lázaro Izquirerda 2007, p. 31; according to Polo the one who does not love his small patria does not love his big one (e.g. Spain) either</ref> Following defeats in successive elections<ref>Manuel Polo y Peyrolón, ''Memorias políticas'', Madrid 2013, {{ISBN|9788499405872}}, pp. 113-116</ref> he resumed his parliamentary career as a senator in 1907,<ref>voted in by the provincial Valencian deputies, Polo was one of 8 Carlist senators, see Cesar Alcala, ''100 ańos de Solidaridad Catalana'', [in:] ''Arbil'' 90 (2007). He ceded his role of the Carlist Valencian candidate for the House of Deputies to [[Rafaél Díaz Aguado Salaberry]], who lost the 1907 campaign</ref> re-elected in 1910<ref>along [[Manuel Bofarull Palau|Bofarull]], [[José María Ampuero Jáuregui|Ampuero]] and Marques de Vesolla (Luis Elío Elío Magallón), Jacek Bartyzel, ''Tradycjonalizm bez kompromisu'', Radzymin 2023, ISBN 9788366480605, p. 695</ref> and 1914.<ref>see the official Senado service available [http://www.senado.es/web/conocersenado/senadohistoria/senado18341923/senadores/fichasenador/index.html?id1=2269 here]</ref> In the upper chamber he continued to defend the position of the Catholic Church,<ref>he was awarded the [[Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice]] order by [[Leo XIII]], Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12; Polo admired the Pope for ''Quod Apostolici'' and ''Rerum novarum'' encyclicae, condemning communism, socialism and anarchism, mcnbiografias.com</ref> especially during the [[:es:Ley del candado|Ley del Candado]] crisis;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.filosofia.org/ |title=Home |website=filosofia.org}}</ref> he was somewhat acknowledged as a dangerous opponent by procedural gimmicks employed by his adversaries.<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 329</ref> Lambasting the others for compromising the party line, he himself engaged in secret talks with the [[Liberal-Conservative Party (Spain)|conservatives]].<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 18</ref>

In the 1890s Polo emerged among the chief Valencian Carlists. He forged friendly relations with the [[Enrique de Aguilera y Gamboa|Marquis of Cerralbo]]<ref>compare correspondence between the two, repeatedly quoted by Fernández Escudero 2012</ref> and a number of other national leaders, gradually becoming a pivotal figure.<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 406; see also Polo's abundant correspondence with conde Melgar, [[Tirso Olazábal Lardizábal|Tirso Olazabal]], Sacanell, [[Matías Barrio y Mier|Barrio]] and others</ref> Personally introduced to [[Carlos, Duke of Madrid|Carlos VII]],<ref>twice visiting the claimant in his [[Italy|Italian]] residences, Polo 2013, pp. 59-98</ref> in 1901 he was considered a candidate for his personal secretary.<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 405</ref> Revealing interest in the emerging workers’ question<ref>see his ''El trabajo y el salario según la doctrina católica'', Santiago 1897</ref> he contributed to [[Acta de Loredan]],<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, pp. 325-6</ref> published the official Carlist program<ref>''Credo y programa del Partido Carlista'', Valencia 1905, see [http://www.carlismo.es/librosElectronicos/PoloPeyrol%C3%B3n.CredoCarlista.pdf here]</ref> and persuaded the claimant to re-organise the party, uniting the military and civil command chain.<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 413</ref> Fully aware of the need to modernise [[Traditionalism (Spain)|Traditionalism]], he appreciated the role of efficient party structures,<ref>Jordi Canal, ''Espacio propio, espacio publico. La sociabilidad carlista en la España de fines del siglo XIX y principos del siglo XX'', [in:] ''historiapolitica.com'' service, pp. 8, 14</ref> building a dense network.<ref>in terms of number of circulos and juntas created in the 1890s, the province of Valencia was second only to Barcelona, far ahead of traditional Carlist strongholds like [[Navarre]] and [[Gipuzkoa]], see Francisco Javier Caspistegui, ''Historia por descubrir. Materiales para estudio del carlismo'', Estella 2012, {{ISBN|9788423532148}}, pp. 32-33</ref>

In 1904 Polo was nominated chief of the Valencian branch.<ref>Polo 2013, pp. 159-166</ref> Personally intransigent,<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 17; he was earlier at odds with [[José Corbató Chillida]], editor of the Valencian Traditionalist review ''Luz Católica''</ref> he was resented by other [[Levante, Spain|Levantine]] leaders, [[Manuel Simó Marín]] and [[Joaquín Lloréns Fernández de Cordoba|Joaquín Llorens Fernandez]].<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 17</ref> The conflict, fuelled by strong personalities, Polo's adamant leadership style<ref>he applied double standards to the internal party discipline, depending whether he was or was not at office, Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 18</ref> and discrepancies between legitimists and {{Lang|es|posibilistas}}, though Carlism is typically viewed as fanatical, in fact it has always been plagued by division between those opting for "malminorismo" and those preferring to "echarse al monte"; Polo tended to side with the latter. His intransigence is credited for preventing the party from amalgamation into ''Union Católica'', ''Lliga'' or other collaborative structures.<ref>see Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 18</ref> Also on the national scene, bedeviled by intrigues among Carlist pundits, Polo's relations deteriorated, including those with Carlos VII and especially his wife [[Berthe de Rohan]].<ref>Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 307; in conflict with the widow, he decided not to take part in the funeral ceremonies of Carlos VII, Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 18</ref> He considered his resignation handed to the new Carlist king [[Jaime, Duke of Madrid|Jaime III]] a purely procedural gesture, and was shocked to see it accepted,<ref>Polo 2013, pp. 289-296</ref> though as a senator he was appointed to national executive, [[Junta Nacional Tradicionalista]], in 1912.<ref>it was Simó representing the Valencia branch, Fernández Escudero 2012, p. 443-4</ref>
[[File:Manuel Polo y Peyrolon funeral.JPG|thumbnail|Polo's funeral, Valencia]]
With no close family,<ref>after the Third Carlist War his brother Manuel lived in Cuba and England, where he died following a horse accident in 1891, Artagan 1912, p. 116</ref> surrounded by books, moths and butterflies,<ref>Polo was also amateur lepidopterist; since the childhood days in Sierra de Albarracín he was collecting moths and butterflies, donated later to Biblioteca del Instituto de Segunda Enseñanza de Valencia, Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 19; Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12 claims it was Biblioteca del Instituto de Segunda Enseñanza de Teruel. He donated his library to Biblioteca del Instituto de Segunda Enseñanza de Teruel, Sanz Ponce 2010, p. 27; his private documentation, including massive correspondence, was donated to Real Academia de la Historia, Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 12 and is invaluable source of information on Carlism of the era</ref> dedicated to completion of his massive memories,<ref>Polo titled his work ''Memorias de un sexagenario''; it falls into 3 blocks covering personal, political and religious issues, and was first published in 2013, Fernando Durán López [review], ''Manuel Polo y Peyrolón: Memorias politicas'', [in:] ''Iberoamericana'' 14/54 (2014), pp. 235-237</ref> personally intolerant and acrimonious, by the end of his life Polo grew into a misanthrope and passed into living memory as a "grumpy old man".<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 17</ref> He became increasingly pessimistic as to the future of Traditionalism, highly skeptical of its political leaders and the claimant himself.<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, pp. 16-17; according to Polo, "D. Jaime Borbón y Borbón, heredero de la Jefatura de esta gran Casa Real, de la legitimidad española y de la representación católico-monárquica de su augusto padre, le tenían sin cuidado los principios, base y fundamento de su posición y prestigio en el mundo", quoted after Javier Esteve Martí, ''El carlismo ante la reorganización de las derechas. De la Segunda Guerra Carlista a la Guerra Civil'' [in:] ''Pasado y Memoria. Revista de Historia Contemporánea'' 13 (2014), p. 127</ref> At one point he considered himself close to [[Integrism (Spain)|Integrism]],<ref>Urcelay Alonso 2013, p. 17; this was a change compared to the 1890s, when he considered the Integrist secession a blessing for Carlism, see Jordi Canal, ''Las «muertes» y las «resurrecciones» del carlismo. Reflexiones sobre la escisión integrista de 1888'', [in:] ''Ayer'' 38 (2000), p. 116</ref> though until his death he remained loyal to the Carlist dynasty.
